issues.description: Commands and descriptions concatenated on single lines without line breaks or formatting separators. This makes the text unparseable and difficult to read.
issues.suggestion: Add proper line breaks between commands and descriptions, or better yet, use markdown code blocks for commands with separate description text. Example: Use triple-backtick fenced code blocks for shell commands.

issues.description: Shell commands are not wrapped in markdown code blocks or backticks. Commands should be semantically marked as code for proper rendering.
issues.suggestion: Wrap shell commands in backticks for inline code (`$ mkdir ~/Hello-World`) or use fenced code blocks (```bash ... ```) for multi-line commands.

issues.description: Hard-coded user directory path with inconsistent placeholder notation. Uses both '~/Hello-World' and '/Users/your_user_directory/' in different locations.
issues.suggestion: Consistently use either tilde notation (~/) throughout or use clearly marked placeholders like <YOUR_USERNAME> or ${USER}.

issues.description: Inconsistent placeholder notation. Line 5 uses '/Users/your_user_directory/Hello-World/.git/' which differs from the ~/ shorthand used elsewhere, creating confusion.
issues.suggestion: Standardize on one notation: either use ~/ throughout or use <YOUR_USER_DIRECTORY> as a clear placeholder for consistency.

issues.description: No section headings or organizational structure. The instructions lack context and markdown structure (e.g., '## Getting Started', '### Step 1: Create Directory').
issues.suggestion: Add markdown headers for better organization. Example: '## Getting Started' followed by '### Step 1: Create Project Directory' with numbered steps.

issues.description: Missing newline at end of file. The file should end with a single newline character for POSIX compliance and standard text editor conventions.
issues.suggestion: Add a trailing newline at the end of the file to comply with POSIX text file standards.

codeQuality.summary: This documentation change has critical formatting and maintainability issues. The README adds Git tutorial instructions but concatenates commands with descriptions on single lines without proper markdown formatting. This significantly reduces readability and violates documentation best practices. The lack of code blocks, inconsistent placeholder notation (~/  vs /Users/your_user_directory/), and absence of structural organization (headings, sections) make the instructions difficult to follow and maintain.

untestedPaths.reasoning: While the README itself doesn't need tests, the instructions could be validated by checking if they work on different platforms (macOS, Linux, Windows). The commands use Unix-style paths (~/Hello-World) which may not work correctly on Windows without WSL or Git Bash.
untestedPaths.suggestedTest: Consider adding a note about platform compatibility or providing Windows-specific instructions (e.g., using %USERPROFILE%\Hello-World for Windows cmd or $env:USERPROFILE\Hello-World for PowerShell).

testCoverage.summary: The README file is documentation, not executable code, and therefore does not require unit tests. Documentation files like README are validated through code review and user feedback rather than automated testing. No test coverage is needed or expected for this file type.

suggestions.description: Separate commands from explanations using markdown code blocks. Currently, shell commands and their descriptions are merged into single lines without markdown formatting, which violates markdown conventions and makes commands difficult to copy-paste. Using proper code blocks with explanatory text improves readability and maintains consistency.
suggestions.before:
Hello World!
$ mkdir ~/Hello-WorldCreates a directory for your project called "Hello-World" in your user directory
$ cd ~/Hello-WorldChanges the current working directory to your newly created directory
$ git initSets up the necessary Git files
Initialized empty Git repository in /Users/your_user_directory/Hello-World/.git/
$ touch README
suggestions.after:
Hello World!

### Quick Start

1. Create a project directory:

```bash
mkdir ~/Hello-World
```

This creates a directory for your project called "Hello-World" in your user directory.

2. Navigate to the directory:

```bash
cd ~/Hello-World
```

Changes the current working directory to your newly created directory.

3. Initialize Git:

```bash
git init
```

4. Create README:

```bash
touch README
```
suggestions.benefits: Improved readability with clear visual separation between commands and explanations. Maintains markdown best practices. Users can easily copy-paste commands from code blocks. Better accessibility for screen readers. Easier version control with meaningful diffs. Scalable structure for adding more steps.

suggestions.description: Extract the quick start guide into a dedicated section. The git initialization instructions appear to be a tutorial distinct from the project's main purpose. Creating a separate section with clear structure prevents confusion and improves information architecture.

# Hello-World

Hello World!

## Quick Setup Guide

### Manual Project Initialization

If you prefer to set up your project manually:

```bash
# Create project directory
mkdir ~/Hello-World

# Navigate to directory
cd ~/Hello-World

# Initialize Git repository
git init

# Create README file
touch README
```
suggestions.benefits: Clear separation between greeting and setup instructions. Better information architecture - users can quickly find what they need. Easier to maintain - changes to setup don't affect main content. Titled section makes purpose obvious. Reduces cognitive load.

refactorings.summary: The README change introduces git command examples with inline comments that significantly reduce readability and maintainability. Three major refactoring opportunities exist: (1) separating commands from explanations using markdown code blocks, (2) extracting the quick start guide into a dedicated section with clear structure, and (3) modernizing the formatting to use proper markdown features like tables or formatted lists. These improvements would align the new content with markdown best practices and the existing README structure.

recommendations.description: Restructure the README to use proper markdown formatting with code blocks. Commands and descriptions are currently concatenated on single lines without proper separation, making the documentation difficult to read and maintain. Implement fenced code blocks (```bash ... ```) for shell commands with separate descriptive text.

Standardize placeholder notation throughout the document. The README inconsistently uses both tilde notation (~/) and explicit paths (/Users/your_user_directory/). Choose one approach and apply it consistently, preferably using clearly marked placeholders like <YOUR_USERNAME> or maintaining ~/ notation throughout.

Add organizational structure with markdown headings. The instructions lack context and organization. Add sections like '## Getting Started' and use numbered steps ('### Step 1: Create Project Directory') to improve readability and user experience.

Consider extracting the setup instructions into a dedicated section or separate document. The git initialization tutorial appears to be distinct from the project's main README content. Creating clear separation improves information architecture and makes the documentation easier to navigate.

Add platform-specific instructions or notes. The commands use Unix-style paths (~/Hello-World) which may not work correctly on Windows without WSL or Git Bash. Consider adding a note about platform compatibility or providing Windows-specific alternatives.
